lessons.title: Cup Series branch
lessons.objective: Learn what Cup fans care about.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Cup is the big league. Everything else feeds into it.

options.text: The Cup Series is NASCAR's top national series, where the biggest names and budgets are.
Cup drivers earn less than O'Reilly drivers.
Cup races are only run on superspeedways like Daytona.

payload.translation: Cup is where the top drivers race; O'Reilly and Trucks are steps on the way up.

followUps.line: Cup is where champions are crowned and legacies are built.
followUps.why: Cup fans talk about the prestige of racing against the best in the sport.

followUps.line: Many drivers climb from short tracks to Trucks, then O'Reilly, then Cup.
followUps.why: The series ladder matters in NASCAR culture, and Cup is the destination.

payload.prompt: How many points races make up a Cup Series season?

options.text: 26 races
36 races
16 races

explanation.correct: Right. Cup runs 36 points races: 26 in the regular season, then 10 more in the Chase for the top 16 in points.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season is 26 races, and 16 is the number of drivers in the Chase. Add the ten Chase races and a Cup season is 36 points races.

payload.prompt: A Cup field has {{cars}} cars: 36 charter teams plus four open-car spots.
payload.template: A Cup field has {{cars}} cars: 36 charter teams plus four open-car spots.

explanation.correct: Yes. 36 charters guarantee a starting spot, and the four open spots go to the fastest teams that do not hold a charter. That makes a 40-car field.
explanation.incorrect: 36 charters plus four open-car spots adds up to 40 cars, the standard Cup field.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: The top 16 in points make the Chase and we start fresh.

options.text: The Chase is ten races for the top 16, and their points are reset by seed.
Only the top 4 drivers make the Chase.
Winning a race automatically puts you in the Chase.

payload.translation: The 2026 Chase is ten races for the top 16 drivers; your regular-season finish sets your starting points.

followUps.line: The regular season still matters: it sets the seeding, and the top seed starts 25 points ahead of second.
followUps.why: It shows you know the reset gives a small head start, not an automatic title.

payload.prompt: Can a team without a charter still race in Cup?

scene.alt: A Cup starting grid with some cars marked as open entries.

explanation.correct: Yes. Four spots in the 40-car field are open, so a team without a charter can race if it is fast enough to qualify.
explanation.incorrect: Charters guarantee a spot for 36 cars, but four open spots go to non-charter teams that qualify on speed.

lessons.title: O'Reilly Series branch
lessons.objective: Learn what O'Reilly fans care about.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He came up through Trucks, now he is racing O'Reilly before the jump to Cup.

options.text: O'Reilly is the middle rung, where drivers prove themselves before Cup.
O'Reilly is a lower series than Trucks.
Drivers never move from O'Reilly to Cup.

payload.translation: O'Reilly is where rising drivers and some Cup regulars race; it is the middle step on the ladder.

followUps.line: Some Cup drivers also run O'Reilly races on Cup weekends, within NASCAR's limits.
followUps.why: It shows you know the series mixes future stars with established names.

followUps.line: A driver's O'Reilly record tells you a lot about their path to the top.
followUps.why: An O'Reilly title is a career milestone that fans respect.

payload.prompt: What kind of drivers does the O'Reilly series attract?

options.text: Only drivers aged 18 to 21.
Rising young drivers plus some Cup regulars who race it on the side.
Retired Cup drivers only.

explanation.correct: Right. O'Reilly is where up-and-coming talent learns and where some established Cup drivers race too, which mixes hunger and experience.
explanation.incorrect: There is no age cap at 21 and it is not a retirement series. You see young drivers reaching for Cup and a few Cup regulars racing alongside them.

payload.prompt: How does the O'Reilly schedule differ from Cup?

options.text: O'Reilly races on weekdays only.
It often races at Cup tracks on the same weekend, plus some events of its own.
It uses the exact same schedule as Cup.

explanation.correct: Right. O'Reilly often runs as the support race on a Cup weekend, and it also has a few weekends of its own. That lets some drivers do both.
explanation.incorrect: O'Reilly is not weekday-only and is not a copy of the Cup calendar. It often shares a weekend with Cup, plus has some events of its own.

payload.prompt: Can Cup regulars race in the O'Reilly Series?

scene.alt: An O'Reilly Series garage with a Cup driver's car.

choices.label: Yes, but NASCAR limits how often.

explanation.correct: Yes. Cup regulars can race O'Reilly, and fans love seeing them, but NASCAR limits how many races experienced Cup drivers can enter.
explanation.incorrect: Cup regulars do appear in O'Reilly. NASCAR places limits so the series still belongs to its own regulars and rising drivers.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: She is in O'Reilly now; if she wins the championship, Cup teams will notice.

options.text: Winning in O'Reilly can earn a shot at Cup; a title is strong proof.
Cup teams ignore O'Reilly champions.
O'Reilly wins do not matter in racing.

payload.translation: O'Reilly success opens doors because Cup teams watch it closely.

followUps.line: Many Cup drivers have an O'Reilly title or a strong O'Reilly record behind them.
followUps.why: It is a stepping stone, and fans respect the path.

lessons.title: Truck Series branch
lessons.objective: Learn what Truck fans care about.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Trucks is where the chaotic short-track racing lives.

options.text: Truck races are known for close, bumper-to-bumper racing that rewards aggression and nerve.
Truck racing is the most polite series.
Trucks races have no contact between vehicles.

payload.translation: The Truck Series is known for physical, close racing with plenty of drama.

followUps.line: Truck fans enjoy the raw racing, with plenty of side-by-side moves.
followUps.why: It celebrates what the series is known for without overstating it.

followUps.line: Careers can take off after a big Truck race.
followUps.why: Trucks is a proving ground, so one breakout run gets noticed.

payload.prompt: Where do Truck races mainly take place?

options.text: Only on superspeedways like Daytona.
On a mix of tracks, weighted toward short and intermediate ovals.
Only on flat tracks with no banking.

explanation.correct: Right. The Truck schedule leans on short and intermediate ovals, with a few superspeedways and road courses mixed in. The tighter tracks are where the close racing comes from.
explanation.incorrect: Trucks race at many kinds of tracks, not just superspeedways and not just flat ones. Most are short and intermediate ovals, which is why the racing is so close.

payload.prompt: What makes Craftsman Truck Series vehicles different from Cup cars?

options.text: Trucks have pickup-truck bodies and a different package from Cup cars.
Trucks are slower and use fewer tires.
Trucks are identical to Cup cars except for paint.

explanation.correct: Right. Trucks have pickup-style bodies and their own setup package, so they drive and race differently from Cup cars.
explanation.incorrect: Trucks are not Cup cars with a new coat of paint. They are pickup-styled vehicles with their own package, and they run on the same kind of tires as any race.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: Trucks is entry-level, but the racing is more raw than Cup.

options.text: Trucks is where many careers start, and its close racing can feel rougher than Cup.
Trucks racing is safer than Cup because it is entry-level.
Cup drivers never race in Trucks.

payload.translation: Entry-level does not mean tame: close racing and hungry drivers make Trucks lively.

followUps.line: Some Cup drivers still race Trucks, within NASCAR's limits.
followUps.why: It shows you know the series mixes stars and newcomers.

payload.prompt: Do strong Truck results help a driver move up?

scene.alt: A Truck Series trophy next to a path leading to O'Reilly and Cup.

choices.label: Yes, wins and titles get noticed.

explanation.correct: Yes. Trucks is the entry rung, and a driver who wins there often gets a look from O'Reilly and Cup teams and sponsors.
explanation.incorrect: Cup teams do watch Trucks. Strong results, especially wins or a title, are a common way for a driver to move up the ladder.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: {{driver|Their driver}} is having a career year; the cars are finally fast enough.

options.text: Results come from car speed, team quality, track fit and luck; a good year often means all four lined up.
Driver skill is the only thing that matters in NASCAR.
The best car always wins regardless of the driver.

payload.translation: A driver's season rises and falls with car speed, team strategy and which tracks suit their style.

followUps.line: A great year usually means the car is fast, the team is sharp and the luck is turning.
followUps.why: Fans know that racing success is a mix of factors, so celebrating a good year means appreciating all of them.

payload.prompt: Short-track aces and road-course ringers exist. What does this tell you?

options.text: All drivers are equally good at every track type.
Some drivers excel at certain track types, because their skills fit some places better.
Track type does not matter in NASCAR.

explanation.correct: Right. Some drivers love the bumping at short tracks, others thrive on road courses, and some are magic at superspeedways. Knowing where {{driver|their driver}} shines helps you predict the good weeks.
explanation.incorrect: Drivers have different strengths. Some peak on short tracks, others on road courses or superspeedways, and {{driver|their driver}} likely has a few tracks where the car and the driver click.

payload.title: Talk about {{driver}}'s weekend
payload.setting: After the race, she texts you about how {{driver|her driver}} ran.

exchanges.theirMessage: He finished 8th but led 50 laps. I am frustrated.

replies.text: That is rough. Was the car fast early then faded, or did pit strategy hurt?
replies.theirResponse: Pit strategy cost us track position on a late caution. We had the speed.
replies.coachNote: You asked about the story behind the finish, not just the number.

replies.theirResponse: But he led 50 laps. We should have had it.
replies.coachNote: True, but the real story is why the result did not match the speed.

replies.text: He is never going to win.
replies.theirResponse: That is harsh. One bad day does not erase everything.
replies.coachNote: Be kind about the driver she loves, even after a tough race.

exchanges.theirMessage: The car was fast on the short run but faded. That has been our problem all year.

replies.text: Is the team working on that for the next race, or is it track-specific?
replies.theirResponse: We think it is setup-related. A different track might be different.
replies.coachNote: Looking ahead and asking about the cause shows real interest.

replies.text: They should just make the car faster.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, if it were that easy...
replies.coachNote: Teams work hard on these problems; appreciate the struggle.

payload.closingNote: The best conversations look past the finish and ask about the car, the strategy and what comes next.

payload.prompt: Does a driver need a championship to be respected as great?

scene.alt: A driver celebrating a win in victory lane.

choices.label: No, wins and racecraft earn respect too.

explanation.correct: Right. A title is one measure, but speed, wins, racecraft and big moments earn respect too, and plenty of great drivers never won a championship.
explanation.incorrect: Only counting champions would leave out many beloved drivers. Fans respect wins, consistency and craft as well as titles.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: {{team|Their team}} just brought in a new crew chief; this could turn the season around.

options.text: A crew chief is the strategist and lead engineer, so the right person can change a team's performance.
The crew chief is just the person who tells the driver when to pit.
Crew chiefs do not have much impact on race results.

payload.translation: A crew chief brings strategy, engineering and leadership, so changing that seat can matter as much as a driver change.

followUps.line: Some crew chiefs are known for their track knowledge or strategy calls.
followUps.why: It shows you know the crew chief is more than a pit-call coordinator.

payload.prompt: Teammates on a multi-car team share {{what}} to help each other.
payload.template: Teammates on a multi-car team share {{what}} to help each other.

explanation.correct: Yes. Teammates trade data, setup ideas and lessons from practice, which is an advantage of a larger organization. Each car still has its own crew, points and strategy.
explanation.incorrect: Teammates do not share a fuel tank or points; each car scores on its own. What they share is information, data and setup ideas.

payload.prompt: What does it mean that {{team|their team}} races {{brand|a certain brand}}?

options.text: The brand is just a paint scheme; it does not affect the car.
The brand backs the team with engines and technical support, and fans feel loyal to it.
All NASCAR teams are identical regardless of manufacturer.

explanation.correct: Right. {{brand|Their brand}} backs {{team|their team}} with engine and technical support, and fans often root for the brand as much as the team.
explanation.incorrect: The brand is more than paint. It supplies engine support and engineering help, and it shapes alliances and fan loyalty.

payload.title: Talk about {{team}}'s weekend
payload.setting: After the race, she is talking about how {{team|her team}} performed.

exchanges.theirMessage: We had terrible pit stops today. That hurt both our drivers.

replies.text: Were they slow on the change or did someone make a mistake?
replies.theirResponse: A lug nut problem on one stop and a slow fuel fill on the other.
replies.coachNote: Asking about the specific problem shows you understand pit stops.

replies.theirResponse: It was bad execution, not luck. We have to fix it.
replies.coachNote: It feels like bad luck, but teams own their mistakes.

replies.theirResponse: It was one bad day. The crew is usually solid.
replies.coachNote: Be kind about the people who work hard every week.

exchanges.theirMessage: At least both cars finished in the top 20. We can build on that.

replies.text: That is a good reset for next week. What do they need to work on?
replies.theirResponse: Pit stops, for sure. The car balance was okay.
replies.coachNote: Looking ahead and problem-solving is how real fans think.

replies.theirResponse: Better than last week when we finished 28th.
replies.coachNote: Progress counts, so recognize it even if it is not a win.

payload.closingNote: Team fans care about execution and the whole organization, so asking about both cars and the crew shows you get it.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: {{team|Their team}} has a storied history, but they have been struggling lately.

options.text: Teams have ups and downs; great organizations rebuild. Legacy does not guarantee today's speed.
If a team was good once, it will always be good.
Past success does not matter in NASCAR.

payload.translation: Team history is respected, but racing is won in the present; every year is a new competition.

followUps.line: Great teams rebuild and come back. Their heritage gives them resources and smart people.
followUps.why: Fans support teams through the lows because good organizations can rebound.

payload.prompt: How do track types shape racing?

options.text: Each track type creates a different challenge and favors different skills.
All tracks are identical regardless of size or shape.
Only horsepower matters; track type does not.

explanation.correct: Right. Short tracks demand tire management and close racing. Intermediates reward aero and setup. Superspeedways favor drafting and pack racing. Road courses are about braking and turning. {{track|Their home track}} fits into one of those groups, and that tells you what to expect.
explanation.incorrect: Track type changes how the car behaves and how passing works. Size and shape decide what matters, so {{track|their home track}}'s type shapes the whole race story.

payload.prompt: Match each track type to its racing style.

pairs.definition: Close, bumper-to-bumper racing where tire wear and patience matter.
Bigger ovals where aero and setup matter and long runs spread the field.
Huge, fast ovals where drafting and pack racing rule.
Left and right turns where braking and precision decide the race.

distractorDefinitions: A track where only the pole sitter can pass.
A track with no banking and no corners.

explanation.summary: Knowing a track's type tells you what kind of race to expect, and what kind of driver will shine there.

payload.prompt: At a superspeedway, does the draft help a trailing car?

scene.alt: Cars lined up in a draft on a superspeedway.

choices.label: Yes, it helps the trailing car.
No, it only helps the leader.

explanation.correct: Yes. A trailing car gets pulled along in the draft and can build a run to slingshot past, which is why superspeedway racing is about packs.
explanation.incorrect: The draft helps the car behind. It lets a trailing car close in and make a move, and cars line up to help each other.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: I love {{track|my home track}}; it is my happy place in the NASCAR calendar.

options.text: Fans have favorite tracks for the racing, the atmosphere or a personal connection. Loving {{track|that track}} makes sense.
You should not have a favorite track.
All tracks are equally interesting to all fans.

payload.translation: Every fan has a favorite track for its racing, the crowd or personal meaning.

followUps.line: When it comes around on the schedule, the excitement is part of what makes NASCAR special.
followUps.why: Personal connection to a track deepens fandom and makes the story richer.
